title: Clean Communication for Civic Strength
author: Kathleen Schafer
summary: Kathleen Schafer treats communication as the first leadership skill in her Leadership Connection Model and argues that most people never practice it deliberately. She compares it to eating: constant, but ranging from nourishing to depleting. Her proposal is clean communication, meaning communication that reduces harm, strengthens trust and repairs rather than escalates. She names four patterns that keep communication unconscious: projection versus ownership, naming needs rather than blaming, the cost of unresolved resentment, and listening as an active act. She closes with three practices: check in with yourself first, be clear about your intention, and allow for the other person's inner world.
points: Communication is a practiced skill, not an automatic reflex, and the culture trains us toward speed and reaction.
Projection sounds like blame; ownership states what I feel, interpret and need.
Small truths left unsaid turn two-minute repairs into ruptures later.
Three practices: regulate yourself before speaking, state your intention plainly, treat the other person's feelings as information rather than threat.
quotes: In the Leadership Connection Model, communication is the first leadership skill. Not because it allows us to be seen, but because it is the way anything, indeed everything, becomes real in the material world. And yet, despite how central it is, most of us were never taught to treat communication as a skill to practice.

Right now, we are living in an unconscious communications environment. The culture trains us toward speed. Toward certainty. Toward reaction. And because so much of what we encounter is emotionally charged, it becomes easy to confuse intensity with truth. This is how rhetoric turns hurtful. How teams fracture. How families stop talking. How civic life quietly corrodes.

Projection is when I take what is happening in me; fear, disappointment, insecurity, grief, and place it onto you as if it belongs to you. Ownership is when I slow down enough to say: This is what I’m feeling. This is what I’m interpreting. This is what I need. Projection sounds like blame. Ownership sounds like truth without a weapon.

Resentment accumulates when we don’t say the small truth early. When we swallow what needed to be spoken. When we hint instead of name. When we withdraw instead of clarify. And then, months later, what could have been a two-minute repair becomes a rupture. This is one of the reasons clean communication is civic work, it prevents avoidable fractures before they form.

Listening is not passive. Listening is an action, a signal to another nervous system: You are safe enough to be real here. In a world where people feel unseen and constantly braced for impact, listening becomes a form of healing. Not because it fixes everything, but because it restores dignity.

Before you speak, pause long enough to notice what you feel about what was said, not what you think. If your body is flooded with emotions, your words will carry those emotions. Regulate first. Then speak.
